extracted.intended_audience: information scientists, bibliometricians, librarians, and information professionals designing journal coverage and studying literature-scattering patterns
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and apply Bradford's law and related statistical laws (Zipf, Lotka, Pratt, Gini, Price) to measure concentration/scatter in literatures and to guide journal-coverage and indexing decisions. Covers mathematical formulations, empirical behaviors, limitations, and practical implications for collection design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bradford's law of scattering
rubrics_metrics.description: A descriptive statistical pattern showing that literature on a subject is distributed in a core (nucleus) of few journals producing many relevant articles and successive zones of many journals producing fewer; Bradford illustrated zones roughly in ratios such as 1 : n : n^2 for journal counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bradford's law to identify core journals for cost-effective coverage: a small 'nuclear' set yields a large fraction of relevant items while many peripheral journals contribute the long tail. Be aware this is descriptive rather than precisely predictive; empirical graphs (running sums, log plots) show a linear core but can deviate (see 'droop'). Do not assume perfect 1:n:n^2 proportions in every field—test empirically for each subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leimkuhler's Bradford distribution (F(x) formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal mathematical expression (Leimkuhler’s Bradford distribution) giving F(x) — the fraction of total productivity contained in the fraction x of most productive documents: F(x) = ln(1 + ?)/ln(1 + ?x) (appendix notation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leimkuhler's formula provides a theoretically justified, general Bradford curve and is useful for modelling the fraction of productivity within a given top-x fraction. However, computation and fitting can be tedious; compare fits to empirical data and use approximations if necessary. The distribution parameter is related to subject field and collection completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brookes' simplified Bradford–Zipf distribution (R(n) = k log n / s)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simplified formula for practical use: R(n) denotes the number of relevant papers contributed by the journal ranked n; k is a constant and s (the slope) determines the Bradford curve's straight-line portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brookes' simplified form is offered for practical plotting and to determine where the straight section of a Bradford curve would intersect the axis. It is computationally simpler than Leimkuhler's exact form and useful for operational decisions about journal ranking and expected contributions. Interpret k and s in relation to the collection's coverage and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Droop' in Bradford curves (tail deviation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical phenomenon where the tail of the Bradford plot 'droops' (falls below the expected linear relation), typically beginning at some journal rank (e.g., around the 250th journal in some datasets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret droop as often indicating incomplete searching or bibliographic incompleteness (the line is restored when exhaustive searching is performed). Droop can also arise from other causes; investigate search completeness, time-span, and collection sampling before drawing conclusions about the literature's inherent distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pratt index (measure of class concentration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bibliometric index purporting to measure the degree to which articles in a subject are concentrated among sub-specialties (essentially a two-expression mathematical ratio representing distribution vs. concentration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Pratt's index to quantify how concentrated a subject’s articles are among sub-fields; it can be adapted to measure Bradford-type concentration. Recognize its sensitivity to the collection and that similar measures (e.g., Gini) may give equivalent insight. Use Pratt when wanting an explicit concentration metric, but examine sensitivity to sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gini index / Lorenz curve applied to bibliometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the Lorenz curve and Gini ratio (area between equality line and observed distribution curve divided by the triangle area) to quantify inequality/concentration in bibliometric distributions (e.g., share of articles or citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the Gini index (0 = equality, 1 = total concentration) to compare concentration across subjects or collections. Pratt’s index is noted to be virtually identical in effect to a Gini-type measure. Be cautious: Gini/Pratt values depend on collection size, sampling, and time span; compare like with like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lotka's law of scientific productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: An inverse-square law for author productivity: the number of authors producing n papers is proportional to 1 / n^2 (i.e., of 100 authors who publish once, about 25 publish twice, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lotka's law to model author-productivity distributions in a field, but account for deviations: some studies find different exponents, multi-authored papers complicate counting, and humanities may deviate. Treat Lotka as a useful general model but validate against current, domain-specific authorship practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zipf's law (word frequency) and analogy to Bradford
rubrics_metrics.description: Zipf's law states rf = C (rank times frequency ≈ constant) for word-occurrence ranks; Garfield notes Bradford distributions resemble Zipf behavior and that multiplication of rank by frequency yields roughly constant products over ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Zipf analogy to understand rank–frequency behavior in journals and words; note that only portions of the Bradford curve may conform to a Zipf-like straight line and deviations (e.g., in the nuclear zone) are common. Use log–rank plotting to inspect linearity and identify regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price’s cumulative-advantage (Matthew effect) model
rubrics_metrics.description: A process model in which 'success breeds success' (cumulative advantage), producing skewed distributions of citations, productivity, and accumulation; formalized by Price's cumulative advantage distribution (f(n) formula) and used to link Bradford, Lotka, and Zipf phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret skewed bibliometric distributions as potentially arising from cumulative-advantage mechanisms; this helps explain how core journals or highly-cited authors become dominant. Use the process model to reason about dynamics (citation accumulation, journal prominence) rather than treating distributions as purely static.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using bibliometric laws to guide journal-coverage and indexing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of Bradford, Zipf, Lotka, Pratt, and related measures should guide the design of optimum coverage for indexes (e.g., Current Contents, SCI): covering core journals yields a large share of 'significant' items while exhaustive coverage is costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply concentration measures to pick a cost-effective core set (examples: SCI covers ~3,000 journals; 1,000 core journals may provide ~90% of significant articles). Balance completeness vs. cost: do not attempt to cover 'everything' if returns diminish. Conduct subject-specific analyses to determine where to set coverage cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity of concentration measures to collection size, time span, and sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Indices like Pratt, Gini, and observed Bradford parameters are affected by the size of the literature sampled, the time span of the bibliography, and selection/collection procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing concentration across subjects or years, control for collection size and sampling method. Expect indices to vary across years and sample designs; avoid overinterpreting single-year or small-sample measures as intrinsic to the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical variability and limits of applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies confirm Bradford-type distributions in many fields but controversies and exceptions exist; different datasets show deviations, alternative formulations (Leimkuhler vs. Brookes) fit differently, and some data produce different numerical constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat bibliometric laws as heuristics subject to empirical testing. Try multiple formulations, examine fit quality, and investigate causes of deviation (incomplete search, field heterogeneity, publication practices) before generalizing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical diagnostics for Bradford/Zipf-like behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Plotting running sums of articles against journal rank (often log-scaled) reveals Bradford curves; Lorenz curves visualize concentration; inspection of straight-line segments and droop helps diagnose behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use log plots and running totals to identify nuclear/core regions and linear Bradford segments; inspect Lorenz curves for concentration and compute Gini. Graphical inspection complements parametric fitting and helps spot anomalies such as droop or non-linearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical selection of formulae based on tractability
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex exact formulae (e.g., Leimkuhler) may be theoretically preferable but computationally tedious; simplified forms (e.g., Brookes') are often used for operational bibliographic tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical indexing and coverage design, prefer simplified, easy-to-fit formulations when they give acceptable approximation to empirical data; for theoretical or precise modelling use the more exact forms and be prepared for heavier computation.
